rationale: 808 member IDs, titles and original abstract bodies agree in the structured source and PMC HTML. Four saliva-related members cover phagophobia, adverse effects, drug monitoring and clozapine sialorrhea without a Parkinson food comparison.
The chapter summarizes the clinical use of an alkaloid in drooling. It does not report a tested culinary preparation or a raw-fig intervention.
Drooling appears in the background description of acute medication poisoning. The trial evaluates a different population, intervention and outcome.
A pediatric inherited movement-disorders review mentions excessive drooling in a distinct neurological syndrome. No raw fig or Parkinson-specific drooling comparison.
A progressive supranuclear palsy case records drooling as one of multiple signs. The case has no measured food intervention or Parkinson disease comparison.

Fox Insight Table 3 records 26 drooling-class accounts among selected bothersome off-period responses. Free-text mentions measure symptom importance among respondents, with no graded direction after raw fig.
Children with and without molar incisor hypomineralization provided saliva for a proteomics comparison. The study does not measure Parkinson drooling.
Drooling appears in a Wilson disease case table. The original does not report a Parkinson or raw-fig comparison.
A genetically defined juvenile parkinsonism case reports less drooling after a clinical medication intervention. Its ungraded observation and exposure do not transfer to raw fig.

The screening questionnaire includes drooling among possible enrollment complaints. Instrumental airway invasion across 135 swallows from 14 participants is the outcome. No graded drooling or fig effect.
The late-stage review lists clinical management of sialorrhea in a symptom table. No measured culinary exposure or separate raw-fig result.
A clinical summary table lists pharmaceutical options for drooling without a new exposure comparison. It does not report raw fig.
The interdisciplinary review distinguishes saliva escape and dry mouth and mentions oral-care approaches. It does not present a primary raw-fig comparison.
The ALS management article describes oral secretions and a different-diagnosis mealtime narrative. No Parkinson raw-fig comparison.
The 2020 pipeline review identifies sialorrhea as a trial-development target. No raw-fig trial or measured clinical effect is presented.
The visual-dysfunction review lists sialorrhea as a possible treatment adverse effect. No underlying raw-fig dietary comparison.

Figure 2 maps 15 GBA-Parkinson interviews and separately codes seven excessive drooling or saliva reports, five oral dryness reports and four chewing or swallowing difficulties. No food-assigned effect.
The multiple system atrophy review provides a nonpharmacologic table with gum, lozenges, papaya or grape-seed extract. The table offers no dose, comparator, numerical sialorrhea result or raw fig.
The autonomic review discusses care approaches and separately describes dietary cueing with gum or hard candy. It presents no new graded drooling comparison or raw fig.
The orthostatic review lists sialorrhea among possible cholinergic adverse effects. No dietary comparison or Parkinson drooling effect.
The Korean translation paper estimates whole-scale model and translation performance. It does not report a separate graded drooling response to food.
The social isolation analysis discusses drooling as a possible public eating barrier. The exposure is isolation. The original does not measure an ingredient effect on drooling.
The fourth anterocollis case with cerebellar degeneration reported less drooling and easier swallowing after treatment. No Parkinson diagnosis, food comparison or graded drooling endpoint.
The autism review mentions drooling among adverse effects. It is a different diagnosis and pharmacologic context.
The animal model review lists drooling among human clinical symptoms in background text. It does not present a dietary or primary clinical drooling estimate.
The chemistry article names drooling in its clinical introduction. The study outcome is an impurity identification, without a dietary or patient symptom comparison.
This pathology review includes drooling among advanced multiple system atrophy manifestations and describes multiple different diagnoses. No assigned culinary exposure or effect.
